report:
Based on strong, converging evidence, the answer is actually **no** — arthroscopy does not meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis, contrary to the premise in your question.

## What the evidence shows

**High-quality randomized trials consistently find no benefit.** Moseley's landmark placebo-controlled trial found outcomes after arthroscopic lavage or debridement were no better than a sham surgical procedure (https://forums.studentdoctor.net/threads/giving-it-a-shot-oa-of-the-knee.149856/). Kirkley et al.'s single-center RCT in the *New England Journal of Medicine* compared arthroscopic surgery plus optimized medical/physical therapy to medical/physical therapy alone in moderate-to-severe knee OA and found no significant difference in outcomes at two years (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

**Systematic reviews and meta-analyses confirm this.** A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis in *BMJ* concluded arthroscopic surgery (partial meniscectomy, debridement, or both) provides no clinically important benefit over conservative treatment for degenerative knee disease, including OA, while carrying documented harms (e.g., infection, DVT); the authors recommended against the practice for middle-aged and older patients (https://www.bjsm.bmj.com/content/49/19/1229). This finding was reaffirmed by an updated Cochrane review (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease) and a more recent 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis concluding arthroscopic surgery is not superior to conservative treatment for knee OA (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3).

## Bottom line

The weight of high-quality evidence — placebo-controlled trials, RCTs, and multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses — indicates arthroscopy does **not** provide meaningful benefit for knee osteoarthritis beyond conservative therapy, and major clinical guidelines now recommend against it for this indication.
